overview: This two-page memorandum records an April 13, 1935 conversation concerning jurisdiction over a homicide aboard the Japanese steamship RASHIN MARU. A Chinese seaman allegedly killed another Chinese seaman about ten miles from Hawaii, after which the vessel’s master reported the case upon arriving at Honolulu. Japanese Embassy representative Shun-ichiro Kawahara sought clarification of the accused man’s custody and prospective deportation to Japan, while the Department of Justice concluded that no federal law appeared to have been violated and left any question under Hawaiian territorial law to the territorial authorities.

people.name: Eugene H. Dooman
people.role: Department of State official in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs; participant and apparent author of the memorandum

people.name: Mr. Ramsay
people.role: Official of the Criminal Division, Department of Justice

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on the RASHIN MARU homicide
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records diplomatic and interdepartmental discussions over custody and jurisdiction following the killing of a Chinese seaman aboard the Japanese steamship RASHIN MARU near Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Shun-ichiro Kawahara reported that one Chinese seaman had killed another aboard the RASHIN MARU approximately ten miles from Hawaii and that the vessel’s master had reported the incident to the Japanese Consulate General after arriving at Honolulu. The consul general wanted the accused held until he could be deported to Japan for trial, but the United States District Attorney delayed the vessel’s departure pending instructions from the Department of Justice. Mr. Ramsay told Dooman that Justice had found no apparent violation of federal law, had left possible violations of Hawaiian territorial law to the territorial authorities, and had advised that the master could resume custody of the accused at any time. Kawahara expressed appreciation after Dooman relayed this information.

interest: The memorandum provides a concise case study of the uncertain division of criminal jurisdiction among federal, territorial, consular, and flag-state authorities in a homicide committed near Hawaii before statehood. It is particularly useful for showing how diplomatic officials resolved practical questions of custody and a ship’s departure through informal telephone consultation. The document also illuminates the legally and politically complex position of Chinese crewmen aboard a Japanese vessel and the contemplated removal of the accused to Japan for trial.
